summary: Declares RFC 1264, which prescribed rules to protect the Internet from new routing protocols with undesirable properties, obsolete. The Internet now has many other pressures against deploying unreasonable protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: An old rule said new routing protocols needed a special check. Today there are plenty of other reasons not to use a bad one, so the old rule is retired.

questions: why were routing protocol rules dropped
subtitle: The IETF retires RFC 1264, the extra rules for publishing routing protocols, because they now just get in the way.

tldr.problem: RFC 1264 imposed extra requirements (implementation, MIBs, security) on routing protocols seeking the IETF Standards Track, which slowed publication.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4794 reclassifies RFC 1264 as Historic, leaving the general rules of RFC 2026, under which the IESG can already require implementation experience.
tldr.outcome: The blanket requirement for all routing documents is gone. Working groups may keep their own stricter procedures.

today: RFC 4794 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1264 by reclassifying it as historic. It has not been obsoleted itself.

sections.title: What RFC 1264 Required
sections.content:
RFC 1264 described rules for publishing routing protocols on the IETF Standards Track, including requirements for implementation, MIBs and security. They were written to protect the Internet from incomplete or unscalable new protocols.

The author says RFC 1264 was written during what was effectively a completely different time in the life of the Internet. Today there are so many other pressures against deploying unreasonable protocols that existing controls suffice, and the rules just get in the way.
sections.plainLanguage: Long ago, routing protocols had to pass an extra inspection. Now there are many other reasons nobody would use a bad one, so the extra inspection just slows things down.

sections.title: Why It Is Obsolete
sections.content:
The memo names timeliness as one of the big problems the IETF faces, and says extra rules for one class of protocols hurt the ability to publish on time. The standard process in RFC 2026 already lets the IESG require implementation and/or operational experience for a Proposed Standard that materially affects core Internet protocols or has significant operational impact.

The document therefore reclassifies RFC 1264 as historic. The Routing Area Directors can still require such experience under RFC 2026, but the broad, general requirement on all routing documents is removed. The authors had tried to write an updated version of the rules and abandoned the effort when they concluded there was no way to write them so that they advanced the IETF's goals.
sections.plainLanguage: The general rule book already lets the referee ask for proof when it matters. So a second rule book just for routing is dropped.

sections.title: Working Groups and Manageability
sections.content:
Some Routing Area working groups developed procedures based on RFC 1264, such as requiring implementations before sending a document to the IESG. This action does not stop them from continuing, and the memo encourages working groups to put measures in place to improve the quality of their output.

RFC 1264 required a MIB module to be in development. That is still encouraged in a broad sense, but manageability should be considered in the context of current IETF management protocols. A "Manageability Requirements" section is described in a work-in-progress draft; it is not currently a requirement but should be considered. For security, current policies such as the requirement for a Security Considerations section suffice.
sections.plainLanguage: Teams that like the old checks may keep them. Thinking about how to look after your protocol is still a good idea, but it is no longer a must.

references.text: Hinden, R., "Internet Engineering Task Force Internet Routing Protocol Standardization Criteria", RFC 1264, October 1991.
Bradner, S., "The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3", BCP 9, RFC 2026, October 1996.
